channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Boston Scientific reaches day nine with plants still disrupted — an IT breach that never touched a PLC
item.description: Nine days after detecting an intrusion on 25 August, Boston Scientific still has no full restoration date. Manufacturing, order processing and global shipping remain disrupted, with EDI and GHX orders queuing unfulfilled. In its 30 August update the company said investigators have found no signs of malicious activity in its environment since detection, that the unauthorised access appears confined to certain on-premise systems rather than cloud, and that it hopes to resume shipping at least some products this week. CrowdStrike and other responders remain engaged. Implanted cardiac devices and established remote monitoring are unaffected. No entry route, vulnerability or ransomware involvement has been named, and no group has credibly claimed it. For OT defenders that is the whole lesson: an enterprise-side compromise that never reached a controller has now stopped production for over a week. - Boston Scientific incident page and SEC filing, plus SecurityWeek’s recovery reporting — also covered by MedTech Dive, TechCrunch, Supply Chain Dive and CBS News - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; manufacturing disruption confirmed 28 Aug 2026; company update 30 Aug 2026; still disrupted at 31 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026, 12:35 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, quantified: 100+ exposed systems, and an attack surface no asset register had recorded
item.category: Campaign — Confirmed OT disruption, water sector
item.description: July’s wave against US water utilities is the best-documented OT campaign of the year, and CISA has now put a figure on it: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem, with targeting reported across at least a dozen states including Minnesota, Michigan, South Dakota, Georgia, New Jersey and Alabama. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, some degrading operations — lost pressure, flooding, forced manual running — though supply was not widely interrupted. In some intrusions actors modified PLCs to disable shutdown processes and alarms, allowing unsafe conditions to develop unannounced. US officials assess Iranian actors as likely responsible and describe the activity as largely opportunistic. What makes this the board’s most useful item is the admission behind the number: the exposure that enabled it was in nobody’s asset register. - CISA exposure-reduction guidance and the FBI/EPA public service announcement — corroborated by SecurityWeek, TechCrunch and The Register - Scale confirmed and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA issued late July 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Attackers crossed from a wind farm into a heat-and-power plant over a private APN — and tripped the steam turbine
item.category: CERT Polska follow-up report — Confirmed OT manipulation, energy sector
item.description: CERT Polska has published its follow-up report on a 29 December 2025 intrusion at a Polish combined heat and power plant serving heat to roughly 50,000 residents, and the entry path is one nobody had documented before. The attackers reached the plant’s OT network through a private APN — a dedicated mobile network a distribution system operator provisions with a carrier to reach its own remote assets — pivoting in from a separate wind farm that shared it. A misconfiguration allowed any device on that APN to open a connection to any other, so what was assumed to be a point-to-point telemetry link behaved as a flat network. Inside, the actors shut down a steam turbine and the water treatment system producing process water, interrupting cogeneration. CERT Polska surveyed other Polish operators and found the same permissive configuration was common. - CERT Polska follow-up report — also covered by Help Net Security, BleepingComputer and The Hacker News - Incident 29 Dec 2025; CERT Polska report published Aug 2026, reported 11 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026, 12:35 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] NCSC: OT targeting is up across sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
item.category: Agency warning — Cross-sector OT targeting, real-world disruption
item.description: The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre published a statement on 27 August saying it is seeing increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors worldwide, including in the UK, carried out by a range of threat actors, and that this has already produced limited real-world disruption. The agency ties it to a broader pattern of disruptive activity against internet-exposed systems and edge devices — routers, gateways and firewalls that hand an attacker a foothold. Its asks are concrete: keep an accurate inventory of internet-facing systems, understand what each edge device does and where its data flows, patch promptly, retire end-of-life equipment, disable Telnet and SNMP v1/v2, and watch for unexpected configuration changes or outbound connections. Coming a day after CISA’s exposure guidance, this is two national agencies independently reaching the same conclusion in the same week. - UK NCSC news statement — corroborated by GovInfoSecurity and CircleID - Published 27 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A small UK generating station ran manually for four days after an Iran-linked cyberattack
item.category: Incident — Confirmed OT disruption, power generation (UK)
item.description: A small British power generating station was taken offline for four days by a cyberattack, with staff forced to restore operations manually. The Telegraph broke the story on 22 August; the UK government confirmed that a small-scale generator had been affected while stating there was at no point a risk to the national energy system, and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has since contacted power companies about the risk. UK assessments reported by the Telegraph point to hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime, likely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The site’s size is the uncomfortable part rather than a reassurance: distributed generation, embedded generators and behind-the-meter assets sit below most reporting thresholds, are often remotely operated by a third party, and are numerous enough that an attack that works once is repeatable. - SecurityWeek and CNBC, both citing the originating Telegraph report and the UK government statement - Incident occurred July 2026; reported 22–23 Aug 2026; government response reported 24 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Five agencies declare Siemens S7 PLCs an active target — with AI-written tooling disguised as monitoring software
item.category: Joint advisory — Active threat to Siemens S7 controllers, six sectors
item.description: On 19 August the NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA jointly published AA26-231A, describing active threat activity against internet-exposed Siemens S7 Series programmable logic controllers. Actors combine publicly available industrial automation libraries with AI-assisted scripting to produce custom exploitation tools that masquerade as legitimate OT monitoring software, locating targets through internet-scanning services such as Censys and ZoomEye and favouring devices running outdated firmware or default passwords. The agencies report read and write access to PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic, and name critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities as the targeted sectors. Their framing was deliberate: this is an active threat, not a theoretical one, and the use of AI lowers the OT expertise an attacker needs. - CISA advisory AA26-231A — corroborated by Industrial Cyber, Cybersecurity Dive, Help Net Security and Tenable - Published 19 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] A PLC maker for wastewater utilities lost 644 GB — including product diagrams and a customer list
item.category: Confirmed breach — Water/wastewater OT vendor, supply chain
item.description: Micro-Comm, a small Olathe, Kansas manufacturer of programmable logic controllers and SCADA software used by wastewater treatment facilities, has confirmed a ransomware breach it discovered on 31 July. The FBI confirmed it is in contact with the company. A relatively new profit-motivated crew calling itself Barracuda claimed the attack and on 6 August posted what it said was nearly 850,000 files — roughly 644 gigabytes. A file listing compiled by cybercrime researchers reportedly references named government customers including localities and a US military facility, employee names, and product diagrams. The company says the released files held no user passwords or credentials, which customers store themselves, and nothing about its own ability to reach devices remotely, and the FBI told it the intrusion was opportunistic rather than targeted. It is not believed to be part of the Iran-linked campaign against water plants. It is on this board because it is the vendor layer of that same sector, and because roughly 200 of the company’s SCADAview CSX systems in the US answer from the public internet. - Reuters exclusive by AJ Vicens, based on statements from Micro-Comm and the FBI, with exposure data from Censys and analysis from SentinelOne - Discovered 31 Jul 2026; leak posted 6 Aug 2026; first reported 26 Aug 2026 — verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Fire Ant moves from hypervisors into routers and TACACS servers — and switches the logs off behind it
item.category: Threat research — China-nexus espionage, network and authentication infrastructure
item.description: Sygnia reports that the China-nexus actor it tracks as Fire Ant has expanded from hypervisor-level compromise into the infrastructure that routes, authenticates and manages high-value environments: Cisco IOS XR routers, authentication systems and Linux management hosts. Investigators found an active GRE tunnel on a router that the configuration history could not explain, and from there custom malware persisting as a fake system service, selective syslog suppression to hide the tunnel, and interactive shell access that produced no logging at all. The router was not a stepping stone so much as a platform — collecting traffic and credentials while blinding the evidence trail. Sygnia assesses strong overlap with the cluster Mandiant tracks as UNC3886. For OT operators the relevance is placement: this is pre-positioning in the trusted layer beneath the security stack, not control-system manipulation. - Sygnia research blog and press release — corroborated by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News - Published 31 Aug 2026 — verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] The FBI took down the scanner and the relay network — and the victim list runs through critical infrastructure
item.category: Law enforcement — PRC state-sponsored scanning and relay infrastructure seized
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures of the domains behind two linked hacking platforms, QScan and QTRouter, built and run by a PRC state-sponsored group tracked as QTFY and operated out of a Nanjing contractor firm. The pairing is what makes this an OT story rather than an espionage footnote. QScan performed mass vulnerability scanning and automatically compromised large numbers of IoT and embedded devices; QTRouter then relayed attacker traffic through those compromised devices, so intrusion attempts arrived at victims from addresses that looked local and legitimate. Investigators say QTFY stole data from more than 300 US organisations, with named victims including the Department of Energy, NASA, the Federal Reserve and the US Senate, and that its customers included Chinese state intelligence and military organs. Activity is traced back to at least 2018. - US Department of Justice press release — corroborated by UPI and SecurityOnline - Announced 26 Aug 2026 — verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in one quarter — and not one attacker had to touch a control system
item.category: Threat data — Industrial ransomware, all sectors
item.description: Dragos’s Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis counts 1,140 incidents involving industrial organisations, up roughly 12% from 1,020 in Q1, with manufacturing accounting for 747 of them. The finding practitioners keep citing is the negative one: Dragos observed no case in which a ransomware operator reached Stage 2 of the ICS Cyber Kill Chain or directly manipulated a control system. Operational disruption still occurred — through encryption of enterprise and virtualisation estates, or through precautionary shutdowns the operator ordered itself. Dragos also notes the continuing drift of the extortion model from encryption toward data-theft-only operations, and flags Chaos ransomware splitting into a conventional criminal service and a state-linked espionage campaign. The strategic read for an OT programme is that the adversary does not need ICS capability to stop your plant, and your defences should be sized accordingly. - Dragos industrial ransomware analysis for Q2 2026 — reported by Help Net Security - Published 11 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler bug Citrix called a denial of service turned out to be unauthenticated RCE — and the deadline has passed
item.category: CVE-2026-8452 — Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway, CVSS v4 8.8, in KEV
item.description: Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-8452 on 30 June as a memory-overflow issue that could cause a denial-of-service condition. In mid-August researchers at watchTowr Labs demonstrated the same flaw could be driven to unauthenticated remote code execution — a pre-authentication heap overflow in the code parsing SAML single sign-on messages on the appliance’s AAA service, reachable with no credentials and no user interaction. Exploitation in the wild followed the public proof of concept, with defenders observing web shells dropped and discovery commands run on compromised appliances. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August with a federal remediation deadline of 29 August, which has now passed. Affected configurations are Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN, RDP Proxy) or an AAA virtual server — which is to say, the box a great many plants remote in through. - CISA KEV addition of 26 Aug 2026 and Citrix advisory CTX696604 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer and Help Net Security - Originally disclosed 30 Jun 2026; RCE demonstrated mid-Aug 2026; added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; deadline 29 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 27 August batch: a substation protocol test set that can be impersonated, and weak hashing in a robot fleet manager
item.category: ICSA-26-239-01 to -05 — Seven advisories, energy and water among them
item.description: CISA published seven ICS advisories on 27 August. Two matter most to utility and plant engineers. The Applied Systems Engineering ASE2000 V2 Communications Test Set — used in water, wastewater and energy for substation and RTU protocol work — carries an improper certificate validation flaw in versions 2.35 through 2.37 that could let an attacker impersonate a trusted peer, complete the TLS handshake and read or modify protected communications, alongside an inherited Apache log4net XXE issue affecting 2.25 through 2.37. Upgrading to 2.38 or later resolves both. Separately, Rockwell Automation’s OTTO Fleet Manager, at V2.36.2 and prior, used an insufficient bcrypt work factor, lowering the cost of offline brute-force against stored password hashes; CVSS v3 6.8, fixed in 2.36.3. The rest of the batch covers Mitsubishi Electric FA products and CNC series updates plus several small gateway and fuel-management products. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-239-04 and the 27 Aug 2026 batch — corroborated by the WaterISAC TLP:CLEAR bulletin and ISSSource - Published 27 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Nine more ICS advisories, including a Siemens edge gateway used in energy and a Class B AIS transponder
item.category: 25 August batch — Nine advisories, energy and marine among them
item.description: The 25 August batch of nine CISA ICS advisories is the wider of the two published last week. Energy-relevant entries include Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced — the edge gateway family for which Siemens disclosed a high-severity authentication-bypass allowing a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute code with elevated privileges — and the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial device server. Marine operators should note the Furuno FA-50 Class B AIS transponder advisory. The batch also covers Optigo Networks’ Visual BACnet capture tools (Update A) and Lantronix EDS3000PS/EDS5000 (Update A), both building-automation and serial-to-Ethernet staples, plus Rently Smart Home, ZoneMinder, PayRange API and the Bendix EC80 brake ECU. The common thread across the serial servers and edge gateways is that these are precisely the small boxes that quietly bridge a legacy field device to a network someone assumed was isolated. - CISA ICS advisories of 25 Aug 2026, listed in the WaterISAC TLP:CLEAR bulletin — SIMATIC IoT2050 detail from Siemens ProductCERT - Published 25 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] August ICS patch day: ten Siemens advisories, a critical RCE in video management, and an edge-gateway auth bypass
item.category: Vendor patch day — Siemens, Schneider Electric, Phoenix Contact
item.description: Siemens, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact released their August 2026 ICS patch-day updates together. Siemens issued ten new advisories. The one rated critical is a remote code execution flaw in Siveillance Video management servers — physical security infrastructure that in practice sits on plant and campus networks and is often administered outside the OT patch programme. The high-severity entries include the SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced authentication bypass, which allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges on the underlying server, plus issues in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid, the Siemens License Server and LOGO!. The engineering-software items are the ones most often deferred and most often installed on machines with direct control-network access. - Siemens ProductCERT August 2026 advisories, with the batch summarised in ICS Patch Tuesday coverage — Siveillance Video advisory also published through CISA - Published 11 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Eleven KEV additions in eight days — decade-old server bugs, and a print server that reaches everywhere
item.category: KEV additions — Eleven exploited flaws catalogued in eight days
item.description: CISA catalogued eleven actively exploited vulnerabilities between 24 August and 31 August. The 26 August tranche of six is instructive in composition: alongside the Citrix NetScaler flaw sit CVE-2015-3246 in Red Hat libuser, CVE-2015-5287 in Red Hat’s automatic bug reporting tool, CVE-2019-1068 in Microsoft SQL Server, CVE-2021-23758 in Ajax.NET Professional and CVE-2022-0995, a Linux kernel out-of-bounds write. On 27 August came CVE-2023-49105 in ownCloud, a Linux kernel issue tracked as CVE-2026-53362, and CVE-2026-66384 in JFrog Artifactory. The newest pair, added 31 August, are the ones to look at first: CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 in PaperCut NG/MF, a missing-authentication flaw chained with unsafe reflection to give an unauthenticated attacker code execution in the print server’s process context. Print management is exactly the kind of shared service that sits on a flat corporate segment with routes into plant networks, and the federal remediation date is 14 September. - CISA KEV catalogue additions of 26, 27 and 31 Aug 2026 — corroborated by The Hacker News and Rapid7 - Added 24–31 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A national emergency over foreign grid equipment — and it reaches the firmware, not just the transformer
item.category: Executive Order 14420 — Bulk-power system supply chain, US
item.description: On 26 August the President signed Executive Order 14420, declaring a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act with respect to foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment. The order covers high-voltage infrastructure at or above 69 kV — transformers, inverters, generators and battery energy storage — and explicitly extends to associated software, firmware and remote-access capability. It prohibits transactions initiated after 26 August involving acquisition, importation, transfer or installation of covered equipment tied to designated foreign entities where the transaction poses a sabotage or disruption risk, and directs the Department of Energy to issue implementing rules within 120 days. Those rules may condition the continued operation of equipment already energised, and potentially require removal. For utilities this becomes a supply-chain compliance layer on top of NERC CIP-013, and it lands on a provenance record most operators do not have. - White House presidential action and fact sheet — legal analysis from Morgan Lewis and Troutman Pepper Locke; reporting from Utility Dive - Signed 26 Aug 2026; DOE implementing rules due within 120 days, by late Dec 2026 — verified 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA has written down the method it wants you to use to find your own exposed controllers
item.category: CISA Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance — Guidance, all sectors
item.description: Issued on 27 August and built directly on the July water campaign, CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance is the first federal document that tells OT operators, in operational detail, how to audit their own external attack surface. It is explicit that exposure reduction does not mean severing remote access — it means removing access that is not needed and hardening what is. The concrete asks: never let a PLC, HMI or RTU answer the internet directly, route all remote access through a centrally managed gateway, firewall or VPN with a monitored jump host and phishing-resistant MFA, and obtain from every integrator, MSSP and vendor the external IP addresses they use to reach you. CISA also names the discovery tools it expects operators to run against themselves — Shodan, Censys, Thingful and Shadowserver — and lists the OT ports to check, including Modbus, DNP3, EtherNet/IP, OPC UA, BACnet, Niagara Fox, VNC and TeamViewer. - CISA Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance — also reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 27 Aug 2026 — re-verified 1 Sep 2026, 12:35 PM ET

item.title: [Medium] The 72-hour reporting clock lands this month — and most OT programmes cannot yet start it
item.category: CIRCIA final rule — Expected this month, 16 critical infrastructure sectors
item.description: CISA has told stakeholders it expects to publish the final Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act rule in September 2026, after a proposed rule in April 2024, a missed October 2025 statutory deadline, a slipped May 2026 target and June town-hall sessions that drew more than 1,200 industry participants. Once in force, covered entities across all sixteen critical infrastructure sectors must report a covered cyber incident to CISA within 72 hours of reasonably believing one occurred, and any ransom payment within 24 hours. For OT operators the hard part is not the form. It is that both clocks start at a determination someone has to make on the plant floor, often from a process anomaly rather than a security alert, and most industrial sites have no defined trigger, no named decision-maker and no rehearsed path from a control-room observation to a federal filing. - CISA rulemaking status as reported by Nextgov/FCW and Federal News Network - September 2026 target confirmed in reporting from Jul–Aug 2026; final rule expected this month — re-verified 1 Sep 2026, 12:35 PM ET
